01 / Introduction

Introduction and scope

Markowitz portfolio theory turns diversification into an explicit optimisation problem: combine assets to achieve a desired expected return with the smallest attainable variance, or select an efficient trade-off between those two quantities.

The central insight is that an asset's contribution to portfolio risk depends on how its return moves with the other holdings. A portfolio is not evaluated by simply averaging its constituent volatilities. Its weights interact with a covariance matrix, and those interactions determine which combinations are efficient.

This guide develops the mathematics of the classical single-period model, explains its economic interpretation, and examines what changes when short selling, financing, concentration and uncertain inputs matter. The original Markowitz paper supplies the historical starting point. The derivations and computed examples here form a self-contained study path, with a live laboratory and worked exercises.

Three levels of analysis

A population problem assumes that expected returns and covariances are known. An estimated problem replaces them with forecasts or sample estimates. An implemented strategy adds dates, trading rules, costs and financing. A beautiful solution to the first problem is not evidence that the third will perform well. Moving between these levels requires additional assumptions and validation.

The model is prospective. The expected return of a portfolio is a conditional forecast for a specified future horizon, not the historical return printed next to a fund. Its variance is a measure of the forecast distribution's spread, not a guarantee against loss. An efficient portfolio is efficient relative to the supplied universe, constraints and moments; it need not dominate assets or risks absent from that specification.

Analogy: designing a team rather than ranking individuals. A team made entirely of people with the same strengths may also share the same weaknesses. Another member can improve the team by performing differently when the others struggle. Covariance measures this interaction. Diversification concerns the composition of the team, not just how impressive each member looks alone.

Notation and reading structure

There are nn risky assets with simple-return vector RR, mean vector μ\mu, covariance matrix Σ\Sigma, and initial capital weights ww. Unless cash is explicitly included, weights sum to one. The portfolio mean is μp\mu_p, its variance is σp2\sigma_p^2, and its volatility is σp\sigma_p. The symbol rfr_f denotes a known simple return over exactly the same horizon.

Part I establishes returns, dependence, preferences and the optimisation problem. Part II derives portfolio solutions and studies cash, constraints and risk contributions. Part III addresses estimation, evaluation, numerical implementation and exercises. Linear algebra and elementary probability are assumed; the key equations are derived and their conditions stated.

The benchmark is deliberately synthetic: annual expected simple returns of 6%, 10% and 14%, annual volatilities of 10%, 18% and 28%, and correlations 0.20, 0.10 and 0.35. The risk-free return is 2%. These inputs are educational assumptions, not current market estimates. Monetary conventions and return units remain consistent throughout.

02 / Return measurement

Investment returns and portfolio accounting

Begin with the cash-flow definition of an asset return. If an initial investment costs P0P_0, ends with price P1P_1, and pays a distribution D1D_1 at the end of the period, its simple total return is

R=P1+D1−P0P0.R=\frac{P_1+D_1-P_0}{P_0}.
(01)

The numerator is the investment gain and the denominator is initial capital. Interim distributions require a reinvestment or cash-account convention. Price-only series omit distributions; adjusted series must be checked for the adjustments they actually implement. A return model cannot repair an accounting definition that excludes part of the investor's cash flow.

Simple versus logarithmic returns

For a strictly positive gross return, the log return is ℓ=ln(1+R)\ell=\ln(1+R). Log returns add across consecutive periods for one compounded investment. Simple returns aggregate across simultaneously held assets using their initial capital weights. These are different aggregation operations:

1+R0:H=∏t=1H(1+Rt),ℓ0:H=∑t=1Hℓt.1+R_{0:H}=\prod_{t=1}^{H}(1+R_t),\qquad \ell_{0:H}=\sum_{t=1}^{H}\ell_t.
(02)

A portfolio log return is generally ln(1+wTR)\ln(1+w^\mathsf{T}R), not wTℓw^\mathsf{T}\ell. Using a covariance matrix of log returns with a linear simple-return portfolio identity is an approximation whose accuracy depends on the return scale. The classical formulas below use simple returns consistently.

Initial weights and self-financing positions

Suppose initial wealth is W0W_0 and asset ii receives capital wiW0w_iW_0. Ignoring costs and external flows, its terminal contribution is wiW0(1+Ri)w_iW_0(1+R_i). A fully invested risky portfolio therefore has

∑iwi=1,W1=W0(1+wTR),Rp=wTR.\sum_iw_i=1,\qquad W_1=W_0(1+w^\mathsf{T}R),\qquad R_p=w^\mathsf{T}R.
(03)

A negative weight represents a short position in the idealised accounting model. Short-sale proceeds finance other positions when the net budget is one. The model has not yet accounted for collateral, borrowing charges, margin, stock availability or possible loss beyond initial wealth. Those are economically relevant restrictions, rather than consequences of the covariance formula.

Time horizons and currency

Expected return, volatility and the risk-free return must refer to the same horizon and numeraire. A monthly mean with an annual covariance matrix does not define a coherent objective. For a foreign asset measured in a domestic currency, the gross return combines the asset's local gross return with the exchange-rate gross return. Currency hedges change that exposure and its covariance.

For IID period returns, a sum of returns has mean HμH\mu and covariance HΣH\Sigma. A compounded simple return is a product and does not generally have those exact moments. The familiar annualisation rules are useful conventions for short-period arithmetic statistics; they should not be silently presented as exact moments of compounded annual wealth.

03 / Portfolio expectation

Expected return and linear aggregation

Expected return averages possible outcomes using the forecast probability distribution. Because expectation is linear, a portfolio with fixed initial weights has

μp=𝔼[Rp]=wTμ=∑iwiμi.\mu_p=\mathbb{E}[R_p]=w^\mathsf{T}\mu=\sum_iw_i\mu_i.
(04)

Independence is not required for this identity. Covariance affects risk, while the weighted mean uses only the marginal means. The weights must be known when the holding period starts. A rule that changes positions using information within the period requires an account of the trading strategy and its conditional returns.

Forecasts, realised outcomes and historical estimates

A mean is a forecast parameter. A realised return is one observation drawn from the distribution. A historical average estimates a mean only under assumptions about how past observations relate to the future. Changing investment conditions, sample selection or return definitions can make that relationship weak.

A 10% expected return does not mean that most one-year outcomes will be near 10%, or that the investment earns 10% almost every year. A distribution with rare large gains can have a positive mean and many negative outcomes. Mean–variance analysis retains a limited description of that distribution; its usefulness depends on the investor's objective and the relevance of the omitted features.

Arithmetic expectations and growth

For positive wealth, expected log growth is 𝔼[ln(1+Rp)]\mathbb{E}[\ln(1+R_p)]. It is not the logarithm of the expected gross return. Concavity gives

𝔼[ln(1+Rp)]≤ln(1+μp).\mathbb{E}[\ln(1+R_p)]\le\ln(1+\mu_p).
(05)

For sufficiently small returns, a second-order expansion gives 𝔼[ln(1+Rp)]≈μp−12(σp2+μp2)\mathbb{E}[\ln(1+R_p)]\approx\mu_p-\frac12(\sigma_p^2+\mu_p^2). Dropping the squared mean yields the commonly used small-return expression μp−σp2/2\mu_p-\sigma_p^2/2. Neither approximation is a universal substitute for a distribution-aware growth objective.

Analogy: average speed and journey time. An average summary can conceal the sequence and spread of the underlying experiences. Averaging investment gains answers a different question from measuring compounded wealth growth. A gain of 50% followed by a loss of 50% has a zero arithmetic average but leaves only 75% of initial wealth.

A portfolio example

With benchmark weights 50%, 30% and 20%, expected return is 0.5(0.06)+0.3(0.10)+0.2(0.14)=0.0880.5(0.06)+0.3(0.10)+0.2(0.14)=0.088, or 8.8%. That arithmetic calculation uses initial weights and the same annual horizon for all three means. It says nothing yet about volatility, loss probability or how often the portfolio must be traded to restore those weights.

If all feasible weights are nonnegative and sum to one, the portfolio mean lies between the smallest and largest asset means. Allowing shorts removes that convex-combination bound: the model can extrapolate expected return by financing additional long positions with shorts. The additional expected return then comes with different risk and gross exposure.

04 / Dependence

Variance, covariance and correlation

Variance measures dispersion around an expected return. Covariance measures whether two assets tend to deviate from their own means in the same direction. Define

σi2=𝔼[(Ri−μi)2],Σij=𝔼[(Ri−μi)(Rj−μj)].\sigma_i^2=\mathbb{E}[(R_i-\mu_i)^2],\qquad \Sigma_{ij}=\mathbb{E}[(R_i-\mu_i)(R_j-\mu_j)].
(06)

Covariance has squared-return units. Correlation removes the marginal scales when both volatilities are positive:

ρij=Σijσiσj,−1≤ρij≤1.\rho_{ij}=\frac{\Sigma_{ij}}{\sigma_i\sigma_j},\qquad -1\le\rho_{ij}\le1.
(07)

Correlation of zero does not generally mean independence. Nonlinear dependence, shared tail events and changing regimes can remain. Under a jointly Gaussian model zero covariance implies independence for the relevant components; outside that assumption it need not.

Expanding portfolio variance

Subtract the portfolio mean and square the weighted sum. The diagonal terms contribute individual variances; the off-diagonal terms contribute covariances:

σp2=∑iwi2σi2+2∑i<jwiwjσiσjρij.\sigma_p^2=\sum_iw_i^2\sigma_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j\sigma_i\sigma_j\rho_{ij}.
(08)

Each pair appears twice in the full double sum, which explains the factor of two when the sum only includes i<ji<j. Forgetting it understates or misstates risk. Volatility is the nonnegative square root of this variance, not an average of individual square roots.

Interpreting risk reduction

For positive weights, lower covariance typically lowers the combined variance holding marginal scales fixed. Negative weights reverse some covariance contributions. An asset with high standalone volatility can still hedge another exposure if its covariance with the current portfolio is sufficiently negative.

Low correlation is not the same as low covariance. If volatilities rise together, a small correlation can still create a large covariance. Correlations also need not remain constant in stressed conditions. A covariance estimate captures dependence over a stated sample and horizon, rather than a permanent structural guarantee.

Variance treats positive and negative deviations symmetrically. For a distribution with asymmetric losses or nonlinear payoffs, two portfolios with identical mean and variance can have different tail risk. Mean–variance optimisation does not eliminate the need to inspect loss distributions, drawdowns, liquidity and liabilities when those determine the actual decision.

05 / Linear algebra

Matrix representation and admissibility

Collect covariances in the symmetric matrix Σ\Sigma. The portfolio variance becomes a quadratic form:

μp=wTμ,σp2=wTΣw,1Tw=1.\mu_p=w^\mathsf{T}\mu,\qquad \sigma_p^2=w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w,\qquad \mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1.
(09)

Here 1\mathbf{1} is the vector of ones, and the transpose converts a column vector into a row. The matrix product reproduces every diagonal and cross term. Matrix notation is more than shorthand: it reveals convexity, supports stable numerical solvers, and makes extensions to many assets explicit.

Positive semidefiniteness

A covariance matrix must be positive semidefinite because the variance of every linear combination is nonnegative:

xTΣx≥0for every x.x^\mathsf{T}\Sigma x\ge0\quad\text{for every }x.
(10)

Positive definiteness makes the inequality strict for every nonzero vector. It gives a strictly convex quadratic objective and an invertible covariance matrix. Positive semidefiniteness allows singularity: redundant assets or exact linear relations can create directions with zero variance.

A symmetric correlation matrix with diagonal ones and entries in [−1,1][-1,1] is not automatically admissible. For three correlations a,b,ca,b,c, its determinant is 1+2abc−a2−b2−c21+2abc-a^2-b^2-c^2. A negative determinant rules out a valid covariance structure even when every pairwise entry looks individually plausible.

Scale, conditioning and factorisation

If DσD_\sigma is diagonal with the asset volatilities, then Σ=DσCDσ\Sigma=D_\sigma C D_\sigma, where CC is the correlation matrix. This separates units from dependence and helps validate inputs. A Cholesky factorisation Σ=LLT\Sigma=LL^\mathsf{T} establishes positive definiteness in ordinary numerical use and enables correlated simulation.

Very small eigenvalues create poor conditioning: small changes in inputs can produce large changes in solutions involving the inverse. Forming a matrix inverse explicitly is usually less desirable than solving linear systems. A solver can return a numerically accurate answer to a poorly estimated problem; numerical conditioning and economic input uncertainty are related but distinct concerns.

Singular cases

When covariance is singular, minimisers may not be unique. A zero-variance, zero-budget direction can change expected return without changing risk if it has nonzero mean exposure. That degeneracy is economically significant, not merely an inconvenient exception. Pseudoinverses require feasibility and null-space analysis; they should not be substituted mechanically into formulas derived under positive definiteness.

The live laboratory requires a well-conditioned positive-definite correlation matrix. It rejects invalid or nearly singular inputs with an explanation. The idealised perfect negative-correlation example remains useful analytically, but falls outside those inverse-based numerical assumptions.

06 / Diversification

Two-asset diversification

With weight ww in asset A and 1−w1-w in B, the mean is affine in the weight and the variance is quadratic:

μp=wμA+(1−w)μB,σp2=w2σA2+(1−w)2σB2+2w(1−w)ρσAσB.\mu_p=w\mu_A+(1-w)\mu_B,\quad \sigma_p^2=w^2\sigma_A^2+(1-w)^2\sigma_B^2+2w(1-w)\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B.
(11)

This small example contains the essential mechanism of diversification. When correlation is less than one, portfolio volatility can lie below the weighted average of individual volatilities. The reduction reflects partially offsetting deviations, not a change in either asset's marginal distribution.

Perfect positive correlation

For nonnegative weights and ρ=1\rho=1, volatility is wσA+(1−w)σBw\sigma_A+(1-w)\sigma_B. There is no diversification benefit relative to that weighted average. With short positions, the formula becomes the absolute value of a signed sum; cancellation can arise, but its return implications and financing assumptions require separate analysis.

Perfect negative correlation

At ρ=−1\rho=-1, variance is a squared difference. The nonnegative weight that eliminates the random variation is

σp2=[wσA−(1−w)σB]2,w⋆=σBσA+σB.\sigma_p^2=[w\sigma_A-(1-w)\sigma_B]^2,\qquad w^\star=\frac{\sigma_B}{\sigma_A+\sigma_B}.
(12)

For volatilities 10% and 20%, the zero-variance combination puts two-thirds in A and one-third in B. This is an idealised singular covariance model. It does not imply that a historical correlation close to minus one guarantees a risk-free payoff in future periods. If a genuinely deterministic combination is attainable, its return must also be considered in relation to the available risk-free opportunity and financing constraints.

The minimum-variance weight

Differentiate the variance with respect to ww, set the derivative to zero, and solve:

wGMV=σB2−ρσAσBσA2+σB2−2ρσAσB.w_{\mathrm{GMV}}=\frac{\sigma_B^2-\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}{\sigma_A^2+\sigma_B^2-2\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B}.
(13)

The denominator is the variance of RA−RBR_A-R_B. A strictly positive denominator gives a unique unconstrained minimum along the budget line. The resulting weight need not lie between zero and one. If long-only investment is required, minimise the convex quadratic on [0,1][0,1], which amounts here to clipping the scalar minimiser to that interval. Clipping general multi-asset weights and renormalising is not an equivalent optimisation procedure.

Analogy: balancing two weather-sensitive businesses. An outdoor café and an indoor cinema may react differently to rainy days. Combining them can stabilise total revenue even though neither business becomes less variable. The strength and reliability of that offset matter more than merely counting the two businesses.

Changing correlation while holding means and volatilities fixed is a useful comparative experiment. In real data, those parameters can change together. The plotted family isolates covariance's role; it should not be interpreted as a forecast of which pair of assets will retain a particular correlation.

07 / Portfolio breadth

Diversification limits and factor dependence

Consider nn equal-weighted assets, each with variance σ2\sigma^2 and the same pairwise correlation ρ\rho. Counting diagonal and off-diagonal covariance terms gives

σp2=σ2n+n(n−1)n2ρσ2=σ2[ρ+1−ρn].\sigma_p^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\frac{n(n-1)}{n^2}\rho\sigma^2=\sigma^2\left[\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{n}\right].
(14)

At zero correlation, volatility decreases as 1/n1/\sqrt n. With a fixed positive correlation, variance approaches ρσ2\rho\sigma^2, leaving a nonzero common-risk floor. More holdings diversify the component that is not shared; they do not eliminate the covariance that every pair retains.

Correlation must remain admissible

An equal-correlation matrix is positive semidefinite only if −1/(n−1)≤ρ≤1-1/(n-1)\le\rho\le1. A fixed negative correlation cannot therefore be extended to arbitrarily many assets. Plugging a negative constant into the large-nn limit and obtaining negative variance is a sign that the assumed joint distribution has become impossible.

A factor interpretation

Suppose asset returns have exposures to a common factor FF and residuals εi\varepsilon_i:

Ri=αi+βiF+εi,Cov(F,εi)=0.R_i=\alpha_i+\beta_iF+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(F,\varepsilon_i)=0.
(15)

If residuals are mutually uncorrelated, their weighted variance decreases as capital is spread across sufficiently small positions. The portfolio factor exposure remains ∑iwiβi\sum_iw_i\beta_i, so a portfolio containing hundreds of assets can retain substantial market, duration, currency or sector risk.

Var(Rp)=(∑iwiβi)2Var(F)+∑iwi2Var(εi).\operatorname{Var}(R_p)=\left(\sum_iw_i\beta_i\right)^2\operatorname{Var}(F)+\sum_iw_i^2\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i).
(16)

Factor models generalise this identity to several drivers and residual covariance. Their structure can make covariance estimation more economical, but omitted factors and unstable loadings remain possible. A factor model is an assumption about dependence, not proof that its residual risk is harmless.

Concentration and effective breadth

For equal standalone variance and uncorrelated returns, portfolio variance is proportional to ∑iwi2\sum_iw_i^2. The inverse concentration 1/∑iwi21/\sum_iw_i^2 is an effective number of capital positions for nonnegative normalised weights. It says little about common-factor concentration: ten equally weighted assets can behave almost like one if their returns are highly correlated.

Counting tickers, sectors or funds can also double-count exposure when their holdings overlap. Risk diversification concerns economic drivers and joint outcomes. It may fail precisely when correlations and volatilities increase during a shared stress. Scenario analysis complements the covariance summary by asking which mechanisms could make those exposures move together.

08 / Opportunity sets

Mean–variance efficiency and feasible portfolios

A feasible portfolio satisfies the stated budget and investment restrictions. Its point in the risk–return plane has horizontal coordinate σp\sigma_p and vertical coordinate μp\mu_p. A portfolio is mean–variance dominated if another feasible portfolio has at least as much expected return and no more variance, with one strict improvement.

The efficient set contains the undominated portfolios. This definition is relative to the feasible set and supplied moments. A portfolio can be efficient under one constraint set and inefficient when additional assets or financing opportunities are allowed.

Boundary versus frontier

For each exact expected return, one can find the minimum attainable variance. Collecting those solutions gives the minimum-variance boundary. Under the usual unrestricted, nondegenerate model it has an upper and a lower branch around the global minimum-variance portfolio. Only the upper branch is efficient for an investor who prefers higher mean and lower variance.

A lower-branch portfolio can minimise variance at its own exact target while still be dominated by an upper-branch portfolio at the same volatility. This distinction explains why solving many equality-constrained target problems does not make every plotted point an efficient investment choice.

Random clouds and numerical frontiers

A random portfolio cloud visualises feasible combinations, but a sparse sample does not establish the optimum. Sampling weights uniformly from a simplex also differs from sampling each weight independently and normalising. The plotted cloud is illustrative; its boundary is calculated by optimisation.

Increasing the cloud size may reveal better portfolios without reaching an exact boundary. It can miss narrow regions and corner solutions. A numerical frontier should report constraint feasibility and optimality conditions, rather than rely on how convincingly a curve appears to trace the outer cloud.

Variance and volatility axes

Variance and volatility preserve the ordering of risk for nonnegative values, but change the geometry of plots. A quadratic expression in expected return appears as a parabola in variance coordinates and as a hyperbolic boundary in volatility coordinates. A capital allocation line is linear in volatility along a positive risky-allocation ray, not in variance.

The frontier describes possible trade-offs. It does not identify a uniquely best portfolio without an investor objective, a required return or additional preferences. Calling the highest-return point “optimal” ignores risk; calling the lowest-volatility point “optimal” implicitly chooses a risk-minimisation objective.

09 / Investor objectives

Preferences, utility and model assumptions

The mean–variance framework can be used directly as a preference model or derived under particular distributional and utility assumptions. A common objective is

U(w)=wTμ−γ2wTΣw,γ>0.U(w)=w^\mathsf{T}\mu-\frac{\gamma}{2}w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w,\qquad \gamma>0.
(17)

The parameter γ\gamma trades expected return against variance. It is not an observable market constant. Its interpretation depends on return units, the horizon and whether utility is applied to returns or wealth. Decimal inputs must be used consistently; substituting percentage numbers without changing the objective's scale changes the effective risk preference.

When moments are sufficient

If portfolio returns are normal, their mean and variance determine the entire distribution. With exponential utility of normally distributed wealth, expected utility is exactly represented by a certainty equivalent involving mean minus a variance penalty. This is a specific model of preferences and outcomes, not a statement that all investors should use variance.

Quadratic utility makes expected utility depend on the first two moments for any distribution with those moments, but eventually decreases with increasing wealth beyond its turning point. Its economic use therefore requires attention to the relevant range. A second-order Taylor expansion of a general smooth utility also produces a local mean–variance approximation, with accuracy depending on higher moments and the size of the risk.

What the classical model leaves out

The basic problem is single-period, uses fixed initial weights, and treats supplied moments as the decision inputs. It does not automatically represent taxes, external contributions, changing investment opportunities, state-dependent financing, liabilities, transaction costs or an investor's preference for avoiding specific losses.

Finite variance is necessary for the covariance objective. Heavy tails can make sample estimates unstable even when population variance exists, and infinite variance makes the conventional quadratic risk measure unavailable. Skewness, drawdowns and tail dependence can distinguish portfolios with similar first two moments.

Preferences and dominance

An efficient portfolio is a candidate for an increasing-in-mean, decreasing-in-variance preference. It does not necessarily dominate another portfolio for every expected-utility investor. Mean–variance dominance is a statement about two summaries; stochastic dominance compares fuller distributions under corresponding preference classes.

Analogy: choosing a route by average travel time and reliability. One route may be faster on average but less predictable. A traveller with a strict arrival deadline and a traveller who dislikes ordinary delays may value that uncertainty differently. A frontier lists the trade-offs; a preference determines the choice.

Investment objectives should be formulated before optimisation. A required terminal liability, a benchmark tracking mandate or a downside-loss constraint may be more relevant than an arbitrary target return. Those can often be expressed in an extended optimisation model, but they should not be hidden inside an unexplained choice of γ\gamma.

10 / Mathematical programmes

Mean–variance optimisation formulations

Several related optimisation problems describe different ways to choose a point on the opportunity set. The equality-constrained minimum-variance problem fixes an exact target mm:

minw12wTΣwsubject to 1Tw=1,μTw=m.\min_w\frac12w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1,\ \mu^\mathsf{T}w=m.
(18)

The factor one-half simplifies derivatives and does not change the minimiser. With positive-definite covariance and independent budget and return constraints, a feasible equality problem has a unique solution. Long-only or position-limit constraints can make some targets infeasible.

Exact targets versus minimum requirements

A requirement of at least mm uses μTw≥m\mu^\mathsf{T}w\ge m. If mm is below the feasible global minimum-variance return, the requirement is slack and the GMV portfolio remains optimal. An exact target below that return instead forces a lower-branch allocation. The two problems agree on the ordinary efficient branch when the requirement binds, but not everywhere.

minw12wTΣwsubject to 1Tw=1,μTw≥m.\min_w\frac12w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1,\ \mu^\mathsf{T}w\ge m.
(19)

Risk budgets and penalised objectives

One can maximise mean subject to a variance budget, or maximise mean minus a variance penalty. With appropriate convexity and regularity, varying the budget or penalty traces supported efficient choices. Flat objectives, degeneracy and binding constraints can complicate one-to-one parameter mappings.

maxwμTwsubject to 1Tw=1,wTΣw≤v.\max_w\mu^\mathsf{T}w\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1,\ w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w\le v.
(20)
maxw(μTw−γ2wTΣw)subject to 1Tw=1.\max_w\left(\mu^\mathsf{T}w-\frac{\gamma}{2}w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w\right)\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1.
(21)

These are convex optimisation problems in the standard sense when covariance is positive semidefinite: minimising a convex quadratic, or maximising a concave objective over a convex feasible set. For a risk-budget problem, feasibility requires a budget at least as large as the minimum attainable variance under the other constraints.

Target selection and interpretation

A target should be economically meaningful and expressed in the same return convention as the forecasts. With unrestricted short selling, a mathematically attainable extreme mean may require unrealistic gross exposure. With long-only weights, feasible means lie in the asset-mean range; concentration limits narrow that range further.

The objective and constraints define the answer. Changing any of them changes the problem, rather than merely adjusting a numerical setting. The laboratory reports an exact-target solution and separately states whether it lies on the efficient branch. This avoids labelling every feasible target as an efficient allocation.

11 / Analytical optimisation

Lagrange multipliers and first-order conditions

For the unrestricted exact-target problem, attach multipliers λ\lambda and η\eta to the budget and return constraints. Choose the following sign convention:

L(w,λ,η)=12wTΣw−λ(1Tw−1)−η(μTw−m).\mathcal{L}(w,\lambda,\eta)=\frac12w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w-\lambda(\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w-1)-\eta(\mu^\mathsf{T}w-m).
(22)

Differentiating a symmetric quadratic gives Σw\Sigma w. Stationarity therefore requires

Σw=λ1+ημ,w=Σ−1(λ1+ημ).\Sigma w=\lambda\mathbf{1}+\eta\mu,\qquad w=\Sigma^{-1}(\lambda\mathbf{1}+\eta\mu).
(23)

The inverse notation expresses the algebra. A numerical implementation solves the corresponding linear systems. Positive-definite covariance makes the objective strictly convex, so a feasible stationary point is the unique global minimum; it is not merely a candidate local minimum.

Reducing the constraints to two equations

Define three scalars from the covariance-adjusted budget and mean vectors:

A=1TΣ−11,B=1TΣ−1μ,C=μTΣ−1μ,D=AC−B2.A=\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1},\quad B=\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu,\quad C=\mu^\mathsf{T}\Sigma^{-1}\mu,\quad D=AC-B^2.
(24)

Substituting the stationary weights into the constraints gives Aλ+Bη=1A\lambda+B\eta=1 and Bλ+Cη=mB\lambda+C\eta=m. Solving these equations yields

λ=C−BmD,η=Am−BD.\lambda=\frac{C-Bm}{D},\qquad \eta=\frac{Am-B}{D}.
(25)

These expressions require D>0D>0. Under positive definiteness, Cauchy–Schwarz ensures D≥0D\ge0, and equality occurs when the asset means are all the same. In that case the expected-return constraint supplies no independent direction: only that common mean is feasible under the budget.

Multiplier interpretation

Let f(m)f(m) be the minimum objective value, including its one-half factor. The envelope theorem gives f'(m)=ηf'(m)=\eta. A positive multiplier means a marginal increase in the target raises the minimum half-variance. On the lower branch η<0\eta<0, moving the target toward the GMV mean reduces variance.

The sign depends on the chosen Lagrangian convention. A solver using a plus sign in front of equality residuals can report the opposite multiplier. Compare stationarity equations and objective scaling before interpreting software multipliers economically.

In higher-dimensional constrained problems, this calculation becomes a linear Karush–Kuhn–Tucker system. The same principles remain: define constraint signs, verify feasibility, and distinguish equality multipliers from inequality multipliers. A closed-form expression is useful precisely because it exposes those conditions.

12 / Minimum risk

The global minimum-variance portfolio

The global minimum-variance portfolio minimises variance over the budget plane without imposing a return target. Its first-order condition is Σw=λ1\Sigma w=\lambda\mathbf{1}. Enforcing the budget gives

wGMV=Σ−11A,σGMV2=1A,μGMV=BA.w_{\mathrm{GMV}}=\frac{\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}}{A},\qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{GMV}}^2=\frac1A,\qquad \mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}=\frac BA.
(26)

The weights depend on covariance but not the mean vector. The portfolio's expected return still depends on means when it is evaluated. This distinction helps explain why minimum-variance estimation can be more stable than an allocation that aggressively responds to noisy expected-return differences.

What the objective guarantees

GMV has the smallest model variance among portfolios satisfying the same budget and constraints. It need not have the smallest realised loss, drawdown, tail risk or tracking error. If cash is available, a deterministic cash return has zero variance, so “GMV” normally refers here to the risky-asset universe rather than an unrestricted cash-inclusive variance problem.

The unconstrained GMV weights can be negative. A long-only GMV problem adds inequalities and may have a different answer. In this benchmark the unconstrained weights are all positive, so the two solutions coincide. That coincidence is a property of the inputs, not a general result.

Orthogonality on the budget plane

Any other fully invested portfolio can be written as wGMV+zw_{\mathrm{GMV}}+z, where 1Tz=0\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}z=0. Since ΣwGMV=1/A\Sigma w_{\mathrm{GMV}}=\mathbf{1}/A, the covariance cross term vanishes:

(wGMV+z)TΣ(wGMV+z)=1A+zTΣz.(w_{\mathrm{GMV}}+z)^\mathsf{T}\Sigma(w_{\mathrm{GMV}}+z)=\frac1A+z^\mathsf{T}\Sigma z.
(27)

This proves global minimality directly and explains the geometry: departures from GMV add variance through zero-budget positions. The expected-return impact of a departure is μTz\mu^\mathsf{T}z. Efficient directions obtain that change with the smallest possible additional quadratic risk.

Equal weights and inverse volatility

Equal weights ignore covariance. Inverse-volatility weights use marginal risk scales but do not generally solve the GMV problem. If covariance is diagonal, GMV weights are proportional to inverse variance, 1/σi21/\sigma_i^2, rather than inverse volatility. Correlations alter that simple rule.

Equal-weight, inverse-volatility and risk-budgeting allocations are useful comparisons with different objectives or estimation demands. Their names should not be used interchangeably. A transparent benchmark is valuable even when its inputs are simpler than those of an optimised portfolio.

13 / Frontier geometry

The analytical efficient frontier

Substituting the multipliers into the stationary weights yields the unrestricted target-return portfolio:

w(m)=Σ−1[C−BmD1+Am−BDμ].w(m)=\Sigma^{-1}\left[\frac{C-Bm}{D}\mathbf{1}+\frac{Am-B}{D}\mu\right].
(28)

To find its variance, multiply the stationarity equation by wTw^\mathsf{T} and use the constraints. This gives σ2(m)=λ+ηm\sigma^2(m)=\lambda+\eta m, hence

σ2(m)=Am2−2Bm+CD=1A+AD(m−BA)2.\sigma^2(m)=\frac{Am^2-2Bm+C}{D}=\frac1A+\frac A D\left(m-\frac BA\right)^2.
(29)

The completed square makes the minimum and symmetry explicit. At m=B/Am=B/A, variance is 1/A1/A. Moving the mean equally far above or below the GMV mean creates the same minimum variance, but the upper point dominates the lower one for mean–variance preferences.

The efficient branch

For m≥μGMVm\ge\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}, the minimum-variance boundary is the efficient frontier. Inverting the completed square gives its mean as a function of volatility:

m=BA+DAσ2−1A,σ≥1A.m=\frac BA+\sqrt{\frac D A}\sqrt{\sigma^2-\frac1A},\qquad \sigma\ge\frac1{\sqrt A}.
(30)

The negative square-root branch is the lower boundary. Near GMV, the frontier's return-versus-volatility slope is steep; farther away it approaches a finite asymptotic slope. The axis choice matters when describing curvature or drawing a tangent.

Conditions and degenerate means

The formulas assume positive-definite covariance, unrestricted real weights, a net budget of one and means that are not all equal. No concentration, gross-exposure or turnover limit is included. Mathematical targets can consequently extend beyond the constituent return range by taking large long and short positions.

If all means equal m0m_0, every fully invested portfolio has expected return m0m_0. The efficient choice is the feasible minimum-variance portfolio, and the two-constraint formula divides by zero because the second constraint is redundant. Numerically, nearly equal means make frontier constants sensitive; a solver should detect the degeneracy rather than draw a misleading curve.

Why the frontier is not a forecast of future winners

The curve maps supplied forecasts into optimal model trade-offs. Realised returns can place a portfolio far from its expected point. A frontier fitted to historical means is a transformation of uncertain estimates, not a demonstrated set of future attainable realised outcomes.

Confidence regions for inputs, stress scenarios and out-of-sample evaluation answer different questions from this exact algebra. A precise closed-form calculation can coexist with broad economic uncertainty. The estimation chapters make that distinction quantitative.

14 / Portfolio structure

Frontier weights and two-fund separation

The target portfolio is affine in expected return. Write it as a base portfolio and a zero-budget direction:

w(m)=wGMV+(m−μGMV)h,h=ADΣ−1(μ−μGMV1).w(m)=w_{\mathrm{GMV}}+(m-\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}})h,\quad h=\frac A D\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}\mathbf{1}).
(31)

The direction satisfies 1Th=0\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}h=0 and μTh=1\mu^\mathsf{T}h=1. It changes expected return without changing the net budget. Its positive and negative positions describe a covariance-adjusted exposure to differences in asset means.

Combining two efficient funds

Choose two distinct target portfolios w(m1)w(m_1) and w(m2)w(m_2). Their affine combination has target am1+(1−a)m2am_1+(1-a)m_2 and equals the corresponding target portfolio:

aw(m1)+(1−a)w(m2)=w(am1+(1−a)m2).aw(m_1)+(1-a)w(m_2)=w(am_1+(1-a)m_2).
(32)

Thus any point on the unrestricted minimum-variance boundary can be generated from two such funds, allowing negative fund allocations when extrapolation is needed. This is an algebraic separation result under common moments and constraints. It does not imply that investors with different forecasts choose the same funds.

Risk aversion with a risky-only budget

For the penalised mean–variance objective and net risky budget one, the solution is

wγ=wGMV+1γΣ−1(μ−μGMV1),μγ=μGMV+DAγ.w_\gamma=w_{\mathrm{GMV}}+\frac1\gamma\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}\mathbf{1}),\qquad \mu_\gamma=\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}+\frac{D}{A\gamma}.
(33)

As risk aversion grows, the portfolio approaches GMV. As it decreases, zero-budget positions become larger, increasing expected mean and variance. This risky-only solution differs from choosing an amount of the tangency fund plus cash; the budget restrictions are different.

Constraints break global affine structure

When a long-only or position limit binds, the active set changes. Inside a fixed active set, weights can remain affine in the target, but the full constrained frontier is generally piecewise rather than described by one global two-fund line.

A common mistake is to compute unrestricted weights, set negative entries to zero and renormalise. That changes the target and the covariance trade-off without solving the constrained problem. Two-fund separation is a consequence of a particular feasible geometry; it cannot justify arbitrary repairs to infeasible allocations.

15 / Cash and financing

The risk-free asset and capital allocation

Add an asset whose return over the chosen horizon is known with certainty, rfr_f. Put fraction yy of initial wealth in a risky portfolio PP and 1−y1-y in the risk-free asset. Then

μc=rf+y(μP−rf),σc=|y|σP.\mu_c=r_f+y(\mu_P-r_f),\qquad \sigma_c=|y|\sigma_P.
(34)

For y≥0y\ge0, eliminating yy gives a straight capital allocation line with slope equal to the risky fund's Sharpe ratio:

μc=rf+μP−rfσPσc.\mu_c=r_f+\frac{\mu_P-r_f}{\sigma_P}\sigma_c.
(35)

A fraction between zero and one means lending some wealth at the risk-free rate. A fraction above one means borrowing to enlarge the risky position. A negative risky fraction has volatility |y|σP|y|\sigma_P and creates a different ray; dropping the absolute value would incorrectly produce negative volatility.

What risk-free means

The asset must be risk-free in the relevant return unit and horizon. A bond with uncertain sale price before maturity is not generally a risk-free asset over that shorter holding period. A nominally fixed domestic payout is not fixed in foreign currency or inflation-adjusted purchasing power.

Cash also need not be available at identical borrowing and lending rates. With a higher borrowing rate, the leveraged segment uses a different intercept and opportunity set; the lending tangency fund need not remain the appropriate borrowing fund. Margin and gross-exposure limits further restrict the attainable line.

Selection of the risky fund

Among feasible risky portfolios with a positive expected excess return, the highest Sharpe ratio supplies the steepest positive capital allocation line. Under the standard unrestricted model and the regularity condition discussed next, this fund is tangent to the risky frontier.

The term “capital market line” adds an equilibrium interpretation in which that tangency fund is the market portfolio under shared assumptions. A capital allocation line for an arbitrary investor forecast is already a useful construction, but does not by itself establish market equilibrium or the CAPM.

Analogy: choosing a recipe and then its portion size. The risky fund determines the recipe of asset exposures. Combining it with cash determines how much of that recipe is consumed. This separation is useful when all investors share the same inputs and financing opportunity; different recipes may be needed when those conditions differ.

All plotted cash examples assume the same known simple return for borrowing and lending, with no financing costs or limits. Those conventions make the geometry transparent. An implemented leveraged strategy must explicitly replace them with its actual terms.

16 / Risk-adjusted return

The tangency portfolio and the Sharpe ratio

For a risky portfolio with positive volatility, define its prospective Sharpe ratio using a known same-horizon risk-free return:

S(w)=wTμ−rfwTΣw,1Tw=1.S(w)=\frac{w^\mathsf{T}\mu-r_f}{\sqrt{w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w}},\qquad \mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1.
(36)

This is expected excess return per unit of volatility. A realised sample Sharpe ratio estimates a different, uncertain quantity from historical observations. It must use compatible sampling, horizon and financing conventions, and should not be treated as an input-free measure of strategy quality.

Covariance-adjusted excess returns

Let e=μ−rf1e=\mu-r_f\mathbf{1}. Cauchy–Schwarz in the covariance metric bounds the positive excess-return-to-risk ratio by eTΣ−1e\sqrt{e^\mathsf{T}\Sigma^{-1}e}. The direction attaining the bound is proportional to Σ−1e\Sigma^{-1}e. When its budget sum is positive, normalisation gives

wT=Σ−1(μ−rf1)1TΣ−1(μ−rf1),ST=C−2rfB+rf2A.w_T=\frac{\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-r_f\mathbf{1})}{\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-r_f\mathbf{1})},\qquad S_T=\sqrt{C-2r_fB+r_f^2A}.
(37)

The positive-budget condition is B−Arf>0B-Ar_f>0, equivalently rf<μGMVr_f<\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}. It ensures that the normalised fund has positive excess return and achieves the positive Sharpe bound. Under that condition it belongs to the upper risky frontier.

When the usual formula needs qualification

If B−Arf=0B-Ar_f=0, the excess-return direction has zero net budget and cannot be normalised to a fully invested risky fund. If it is negative, the normalised formula points in the opposite direction and has negative expected excess return; it is not the conventional positive-line tangency maximiser. A routine should not silently label that output as the best positive-Sharpe fund.

Cash-inclusive mean–variance optimisation remains meaningful in these cases: risky holdings need not have total weight one. Constraints can also change the situation. A long-only positive-Sharpe optimum may exist on a feasible face even when the unrestricted positive-budget convention fails. The laboratory reports these cases separately.

Sharpe ratios and portfolio composition

An asset's individual Sharpe ratio is not enough to determine its weight. Covariance-adjusted excess returns can favour an asset with a modest standalone ratio because it hedges other exposures. Conversely, high standalone ratios can belong to overlapping exposures that provide little additional opportunity.

With estimated means and covariance, maximising a fitted Sharpe ratio can amplify estimation error. The ratio is especially unstable when expected excess returns are close to zero or volatility is poorly estimated. Ranking a large collection of backtests by their sample ratios also introduces selection effects.

Capital allocation versus equilibrium pricing

Under the additional assumptions of the CAPM, the market portfolio is a common tangency portfolio and expected excess returns satisfy

μi−rf=βi(μM−rf),βi=Cov(Ri,RM)Var(RM).\mu_i-r_f=\beta_i(\mu_M-r_f),\qquad \beta_i=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R_i,R_M)}{\operatorname{Var}(R_M)}.
(38)

This is a separate equilibrium statement, developed in Sharpe's paper. The security market line uses beta; the capital allocation line uses total portfolio volatility. An arbitrary estimated efficient portfolio is not automatically the market portfolio, and the Markowitz optimisation calculation alone does not prove the CAPM.

17 / Portfolio choice

Risk aversion and optimal risky allocation

Let xx be the vector of risky-asset wealth fractions, with the remaining fraction 1−1Tx1-\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}x in cash. There is no separate requirement that risky weights sum to one. The objective becomes

U(x)=rf+xT(μ−rf1)−γ2xTΣx.U(x)=r_f+x^\mathsf{T}(\mu-r_f\mathbf{1})-\frac\gamma2x^\mathsf{T}\Sigma x.
(39)

Stationarity gives the unrestricted cash-inclusive solution

x⋆=1γΣ−1(μ−rf1).x^\star=\frac1\gamma\Sigma^{-1}(\mu-r_f\mathbf{1}).
(40)

This formula remains algebraically valid under positive definiteness even if the conventional fully invested tangency normalisation fails. The cash weight follows from the total risky budget, which can be positive, zero or negative. Economic financing permissions still determine whether the solution is implementable.

The amount of a tangency fund

When the conventional positive tangency fund exists, write x=ywTx=yw_T. The objective reduces to a scalar quadratic in the risky fraction. Its optimum is

y⋆=μT−rfγσT2=B−Arfγ.y^\star=\frac{\mu_T-r_f}{\gamma\sigma_T^2}=\frac{B-Ar_f}{\gamma}.
(41)

The asset composition of the risky fund is independent of γ\gamma when all moments and financing terms are held fixed. Risk aversion changes the amount invested in that fund. This is the separation associated with the idealised cash opportunity, not a universal rule for investors with different beliefs or constraints.

Borrowing restrictions

If the investor can hold only cash and nonnegative amounts of a chosen fund with no borrowing, impose 0≤y≤10\le y\le1. For this scalar problem, the solution is the unconstrained y⋆y^\star clipped to that interval. If asset-level constraints also apply, the optimal risky composition may itself change and a scalar repair is no longer sufficient.

Different borrowing and lending rates create a piecewise opportunity set. A portfolio between the relevant tangencies can be fully invested in risky assets, while lending and borrowing regions use different supporting lines. A single Sharpe ratio calculated with the lending rate cannot represent every financing regime.

Horizon, wealth and units

If utility is expressed in terminal wealth rather than return, its risk coefficient must be converted consistently with initial wealth. A parameter fitted for a monthly return problem does not automatically express the same preference in an annual problem. Under assumptions that both mean and covariance scale linearly with the horizon, their common scaling can cancel in some allocation formulas, but compounded wealth and changing opportunities need not satisfy those assumptions.

Large y⋆y^\star values can result from optimistic means, small estimated variance or low chosen risk aversion. The equation describes the response of the model; it does not establish that leverage is safe or that its apparent opportunity survives estimation uncertainty.

18 / Constrained optimisation

Long-only constraints and optimality conditions

Long-only investment adds wi≥0w_i\ge0 to the budget and target constraints. The feasible weights lie on a simplex. Exact target means are restricted to the convex hull of the asset means, and the covariance objective remains convex.

minw12wTΣwsubject to 1Tw=1,μTw=m,w≥0.\min_w\frac12w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w\quad\text{subject to }\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T}w=1,\ \mu^\mathsf{T}w=m,\ w\ge0.
(42)

Introduce nonnegative multipliers νi\nu_i for −wi≤0-w_i\le0. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions are

Σw−λ1−ημ−ν=0,wi≥0,νi≥0,νiwi=0.\Sigma w-\lambda\mathbf{1}-\eta\mu-\nu=0,\qquad w_i\ge0,\quad \nu_i\ge0,\quad \nu_iw_i=0.
(43)

Include budget and return feasibility as well. Complementary slackness means an asset with positive weight has zero lower-bound multiplier. An excluded asset can have a nonzero multiplier reflecting the value of relaxing its restriction under the chosen sign convention.

Active sets and corner portfolios

Within an active set, solve the equality-constrained problem on the free assets while fixing bound assets at their limits. Check the resulting weights and all optimality conditions. As the target changes, constraints can enter or leave; the frontier consists of connected pieces with different active sets.

For three assets, enumerating feasible faces is practical and transparent. For a large universe, a validated quadratic-programming solver is more appropriate. A face optimum that violates an inactive constraint is not a valid full-problem solution; neither is the cheapest solution among an incomplete selection of faces.

Constraint cost versus estimation benefit

With identical known moments and the same target, restricting the feasible set cannot reduce minimum variance. The unconstrained optimiser could already choose every constrained portfolio. This set-inclusion argument is a mathematical result, independent of any empirical study.

With estimated moments, an unrestricted portfolio can overreact to errors and have higher population or realised risk than a constrained estimate. This is a different comparison. Jagannathan and Ma study why weight constraints can help estimated portfolio risk. The existence of such a benefit does not mean constraints improve the exact population optimum.

Feasibility and duplicate means

A target at an extreme asset mean may force investment into the assets sharing that extreme. If several assets have the same mean, a feasible face can have a redundant target constraint. A numerical method must handle that rank issue rather than treating it as an invalid economic input.

The laboratory solves long-only GMV, target and positive-Sharpe portfolios by enumerating the nonempty asset subsets. It reports targets outside the achievable range, and labels an exact-target allocation below the long-only GMV mean as dominated rather than efficient.

19 / Investment restrictions

Exposure, concentration and turnover constraints

The net budget and the size of positions measure different things. Define gross exposure as

G(w)=∑i|wi|.G(w)=\sum_i|w_i|.
(44)

A fully invested long-only portfolio has gross exposure one. A portfolio with weights 120%, 30% and −50% has net exposure one but gross exposure two. The net budget alone therefore does not impose a leverage limit.

Position and group limits

Bounds li≤wi≤uil_i\le w_i\le u_i, group exposure constraints and a gross-exposure limit can be added while retaining convexity when stated in standard linear or norm form. For long-only caps, feasibility requires enough aggregate capacity: ∑iui≥1\sum_i u_i\ge1. Lower bounds also require ∑ili≤1\sum_i l_i\le1.

l≤w≤u,a≤FTw≤b,∑i|wi|≤L.l\le w\le u,\qquad a\le F^\mathsf{T}w\le b,\qquad \sum_i|w_i|\le L.
(45)

The matrix FF can represent sector, duration or factor exposures, but the economic interpretation depends on how those exposures are estimated. A constraint on a model factor is only as stable as the model and measurement supplying it.

Trading from an existing portfolio

If the current pre-trade weights are w−w^{-}, the trade is Δw=w−w−\Delta w=w-w^{-}. One common turnover convention is one-half of total absolute traded weight:

TO=12∑i|wi−wi−|.\operatorname{TO}=\frac12\sum_i|w_i-w_i^{-}|.
(46)

The factor one-half counts the combined buy and sell sides once in a fully invested reallocation. Other reporting conventions use the full sum. State the convention, especially if cash changes or external flows are present. Pre-trade weights drift with returns and generally differ from the previous period's target weights.

A cost-aware objective can subtract estimated trading and holding costs, for example ∑ici|Δwi|\sum_i c_i|\Delta w_i| plus convex impact terms. A smooth variance penalty does not represent transaction costs by itself. Cost coefficients must reflect the return horizon and actual tradable size.

Limits of convex formulations

Cardinality constraints, such as allowing at most ten nonzero positions, are generally nonconvex. Minimum trade sizes, fixed fees and discrete lots can also require mixed-integer decisions. A convenient continuous relaxation solves a related problem and needs explicit rounding and feasibility checks before implementation.

Constraints express real investment permissions and can regularise unstable estimates. They should be selected for an economic reason or validated statistical design, rather than adjusted repeatedly until a historical backtest looks attractive. A tighter constraint changes both the feasible set and the sensitivity of the resulting portfolio.

20 / Risk decomposition

Marginal and component risk contributions

Portfolio weights allocate capital; they do not allocate risk in the same proportions. For positive portfolio volatility, differentiating σp=wTΣw\sigma_p=\sqrt{w^\mathsf{T}\Sigma w} gives the marginal volatility contribution:

MRCi=∂σp∂wi=(Σw)iσp.\operatorname{MRC}_i=\frac{\partial\sigma_p}{\partial w_i}=\frac{(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p}.
(47)

The derivative changes one weight holding the others fixed, so it is not by itself a fully funded trade. Moving capital from asset jj to ii changes volatility locally at rate MRCi−MRCj\operatorname{MRC}_i-\operatorname{MRC}_j.

Euler decomposition

Volatility is positively homogeneous of degree one. Multiplying each marginal contribution by its capital weight gives component contributions that add to total volatility:

RCi=wi(Σw)iσp,∑iRCi=σp.\operatorname{RC}_i=w_i\frac{(\Sigma w)_i}{\sigma_p},\qquad \sum_i\operatorname{RC}_i=\sigma_p.
(48)

Variance contributions wi(Σw)iw_i(\Sigma w)_i instead sum to variance. Dividing either set by its corresponding total gives the same normalised risk shares. Keep the units clear: absolute volatility contributions are decimal volatility, while their normalised shares are fractions.

Hedges and negative contributions

A hedging position can have a negative component contribution if its weighted covariance with the portfolio is negative. This does not mean the asset has negative standalone variance. It means that the signed position offsets part of the portfolio's aggregate variation. Component shares can consequently lie outside zero to one in a portfolio with hedges.

At zero portfolio volatility the derivative expression divides by zero. Such singular cases need a separate analysis rather than a fabricated risk allocation. Small-volatility portfolios can also make normalised contributions highly sensitive to parameter changes.

Risk budgeting versus minimum variance

A risk-budgeting portfolio targets prescribed positive shares bib_i, with component contributions satisfying RCi=biσp\operatorname{RC}_i=b_i\sigma_p and ∑ibi=1\sum_i b_i=1. Equal risk contribution uses equal shares. These objectives differ from equal capital, inverse-volatility and minimum-variance allocations.

For independent assets with positive weights, equal risk contribution is proportional to inverse volatility. GMV is instead proportional to inverse variance. Correlations change both results. A portfolio can look balanced in capital while being dominated by its most volatile or most correlated holdings.

Analogy: people carrying a shared load. Giving each person the same number of items does not give each the same burden when the items have different weights and interact. Capital weights count the items; component risk measures how each position contributes to the total burden.

Risk decomposition is a diagnostic, not an independent prediction of losses. It inherits the covariance model, horizon and state dependence of the portfolio variance. Scenario-based contributions can answer different questions when particular stresses matter more than average squared variation.

21 / Statistical inputs

Estimation of expected returns and covariances

Optimisation needs future conditional moments. A historical sample is one source of information, but estimating the inputs is a separate statistical problem. For TT aligned return observations RtR_t, the ordinary estimators are

μ^=1T∑t=1TRt,Σ^=1T−1∑t=1T(Rt−μ^)(Rt−μ^)T.\widehat\mu=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}R_t,\qquad \widehat\Sigma=\frac1{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(R_t-\widehat\mu)(R_t-\widehat\mu)^\mathsf{T}.
(49)

The covariance denominator produces an unbiased sample covariance for IID observations with finite second moments. It does not correct stale prices, missing distributions, survivorship selection, changing regimes or inconsistent currencies. Those affect what the observations measure.

Means are difficult to estimate

Under IID sampling, the variance of a sample mean is Σ/T\Sigma/T. For one asset, the standard error is σ/T\sigma/\sqrt T. An annual expected return difference of a few percentage points can be small relative to its estimation uncertainty.

Var(μ^)=ΣT,SE^(μ^i)=σ^iT.\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu)=\frac{\Sigma}{T},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\mu_i)=\frac{\widehat\sigma_i}{\sqrt T}.
(50)

For an asset with 20% annual volatility, five independent annual observations give an expected-return standard error near 8.9 percentage points. Sixty IID monthly observations produce the same approximate standard error for an annualised arithmetic mean under square-root-of-time scaling; they are not sixty independent years of information.

Longer histories increase sample size but may include older regimes that are less relevant to the next period. Short windows adapt more quickly but have noisier estimates. The trade-off is statistical and economic, rather than settled by always choosing the longest available sample.

Covariance dimensions and missing data

An nn-asset symmetric covariance has n(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2 distinct entries. A centred sample covariance has rank at most min(n,T−1)\min(n,T-1). If n≥Tn\ge T, it cannot be positive definite. Even below that threshold it can be poorly conditioned.

Pairwise missing-data estimation can use different observation sets for different covariance entries and produce an indefinite matrix. A common aligned sample preserves the sample covariance's positive semidefiniteness, but can lose observations. A principled missing-data model can be preferable; silently filling missing returns with zero changes both means and dependence.

Serial dependence and annualisation

For a stationary sequence, covariance of a sum includes lagged dependence. Let Γk=Cov(Rt,Rt−k)\Gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(R_t,R_{t-k}). Then

Cov(∑t=1HRt)=HΓ0+∑k=1H−1(H−k)(Γk+ΓkT).\operatorname{Cov}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{H}R_t\right)=H\Gamma_0+\sum_{k=1}^{H-1}(H-k)(\Gamma_k+\Gamma_k^\mathsf{T}).
(51)

The IID scaling HΣH\Sigma drops those lag terms. Serial correlation also changes uncertainty estimates for historical means and Sharpe ratios. Overlapping horizon returns are dependent even when their underlying one-period increments are independent.

Bootstrapping independent rows assumes row independence. A block or time-series bootstrap can preserve some serial structure, provided block design matches the question. Resampling uncertainty does not capture every kind of regime change or model misspecification.

22 / Covariance estimation

Covariance shrinkage and numerical conditioning

A sample covariance estimates many quantities from limited data. Small noisy eigenvalues can make inverse-based portfolios extreme. Shrinkage blends the sample estimate with a structured target:

Σ~=(1−δ)Σ^+δF,0≤δ≤1.\widetilde\Sigma=(1-\delta)\widehat\Sigma+\delta F,\qquad 0\le\delta\le1.
(52)

A diagonal target removes correlations while retaining estimated marginal variances. A scaled identity target imposes equal variances and zero covariance. A constant-correlation or factor target imposes a different structure. These assumptions should be stated, rather than treating every shrinkage construction as the same estimator.

The bias–variance trade-off

Shrinkage introduces structural bias but can reduce estimation variance and improve conditioning. If the sample and target are positive semidefinite, their convex combination is positive semidefinite. A positive-definite target with positive intensity makes the combination positive definite.

The Ledoit–Wolf paper derives an estimator and intensity under a specified covariance-loss criterion and asymptotic framework. Choosing a convenient 30% diagonal blend is not automatically a Ledoit–Wolf estimator. Nor does minimising a covariance estimation loss guarantee the best portfolio under every objective.

Predicted risk and population risk

An optimiser selects weights that exploit the supplied covariance. Evaluating those weights with the same estimate can therefore look optimistic. In a synthetic experiment with known generating covariance, compare fitted predicted volatility with wTΣtrueww^\mathsf{T}\Sigma_{\mathrm{true}}w. In empirical work, a later evaluation period or another appropriate validation design supplies information about realised risk.

The figure holds the population model fixed and repeatedly estimates covariance from short independent samples. Its shrinkage curve is a controlled illustration. Selecting the best intensity using those displayed test risks would turn them into training information; an honest empirical choice needs a separate tuning design.

Condition numbers and regularisation

For positive-definite covariance, the spectral condition number is λmax/λmin\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}. Large values warn that solving against the matrix can amplify input changes. Scaling to a correlation matrix helps separate numerical units from dependence but does not remove genuine near-collinearity.

Adding a ridge λI\lambda I to covariance corresponds to adding a quadratic weight penalty when λ\lambda has compatible variance units. It changes the optimisation problem. Eigenvalue floors and nearest-correlation adjustments likewise modify inputs and should be documented. They are not merely invisible numerical housekeeping.

Analogy: fitting a map from noisy distance measurements. If each distance is measured separately with error, an unconstrained fitted map can contain implausible distortions. A simple structural template can stabilise the map, at the price of not representing every real detail. Shrinkage uses this trade-off explicitly.

A stable solve is necessary but not sufficient. A diagonal covariance can be well conditioned and economically misspecified. A highly accurate optimiser can then produce a precise solution to an inappropriate dependence model. Statistical validation must accompany numerical diagnostics.

23 / Input uncertainty

Expected-return uncertainty and robust optimisation

Mean–variance optimisation acts on relative expected returns. In the cash-inclusive unrestricted problem, holding covariance fixed, a mean perturbation changes risky holdings by

Δx=1γΣ−1Δμ.\Delta x=\frac1\gamma\Sigma^{-1}\Delta\mu.
(53)

Directions corresponding to small covariance eigenvalues can amplify forecast differences. An apparently small change in one annual mean can produce a large change in holdings, especially when risk aversion is low. Best and Grauer analyse this sensitivity in mean–variance portfolios.

Shrinking or combining return forecasts

A mean forecast can be shrunk toward a common mean, factor forecast or economically motivated prior. This reduces the influence of noisy differences but introduces assumptions about the target. A historical average and a valuation forecast need a coherent horizon and uncertainty model before they are combined.

The Black–Litterman framework combines an equilibrium-based prior with views and their uncertainty. In one Gaussian formulation, the posterior mean is

μpost=[V0−1+PTΩ−1P]−1[V0−1π+PTΩ−1q].\mu_{\mathrm{post}}=\left[V_0^{-1}+P^\mathsf{T}\Omega^{-1}P\right]^{-1}\left[V_0^{-1}\pi+P^\mathsf{T}\Omega^{-1}q\right].
(54)

Here π\pi is the prior mean, V0V_0 its uncertainty covariance, Pμ=q+εP\mu=q+\varepsilon is the view model, and Ω\Omega is view-error covariance. An often used prior form is V0=τΣV_0=\tau\Sigma. In this equation qq denotes view values, unrelated to the dividend yield in the earlier option guides. Inputs must identify whether means are total or excess returns.

The posterior calculation does not establish that the prior or views are correct. It formalises how they are weighted under the assumed uncertainty model. Posterior-mean uncertainty and predictive asset-return covariance are different objects and should not be conflated when passing inputs to an optimiser.

Ellipsoidal uncertainty sets

An alternative asks for an allocation that performs acceptably over a set of plausible mean vectors. Suppose

μ=μ^+U1/2u,‖u‖2≤κ.\mu=\widehat\mu+U^{1/2}u,\qquad \|u\|_2\le\kappa.
(55)

For fixed weights, minimising expected return over this ellipsoid yields

minμwTμ=wTμ^−κwTUw.\min_\mu w^\mathsf{T}\mu=w^\mathsf{T}\widehat\mu-\kappa\sqrt{w^\mathsf{T}Uw}.
(56)

The robust objective therefore penalises exposure to forecast uncertainty as well as return variance. The matrix UU describes mean uncertainty, not necessarily asset-return covariance. The radius κ\kappa controls conservatism and needs a statistical or economic rationale.

Validation and interpretation

Robustness is always relative to a stated uncertainty set or alternative models. A narrow misspecified set can be confidently wrong; an excessively broad set can yield uninformative portfolios. Sensitivity analysis should vary means, covariance, constraints and financing separately to reveal which assumptions drive the result.

Resampling and averaging optimised weights can stabilise allocations, but the average need not be optimal for the original moments or attain a particular target. Each proposed construction needs an identified objective and evaluation. The purpose of regularisation is improved decision reliability, rather than merely smoother-looking weights.

24 / Portfolio policies

Rebalancing and evaluation over time

A single-period weight vector does not fully specify a multi-period investment strategy. After realised returns, a fully invested portfolio's pre-trade weights drift to

wi,t−=wi,t−1+(1+Ri,t)1+(wt−1+)TRt.w_{i,t}^{-}=\frac{w_{i,t-1}^{+}(1+R_{i,t})}{1+(w_{t-1}^{+})^\mathsf{T}R_t}.
(57)

The superscripts distinguish post-trade and pre-trade weights. The expression assumes no costs, external flows or insolvency. A policy must say when new target weights are estimated, when trades occur, and what happens if financing or weight limits are breached.

Buy and hold versus constant weights

A buy-and-hold policy retains asset units, allowing capital weights to drift. A constant-weight policy trades to restore a target. Both can start from the same allocation and later have different returns, exposures and costs. A rebalanced portfolio's compounded return depends on the sequence of asset returns and trades.

The figure compares those policies on a synthetic return sequence. It is not a general demonstration that rebalancing beats buy and hold. Correlation, trend, dispersion, costs and the chosen target all affect the comparison.

Walk-forward evaluation

At each decision date, estimate inputs using information available by that date, form weights, and apply them to subsequent returns. Keep the estimation window, forecast timing, execution lag and rebalance schedule explicit. A return used to form a signal cannot also be earned before the portfolio could have been traded.

Choose tuning parameters on training or validation periods and reserve an untouched test period. Repeatedly inspecting test results and modifying the strategy makes that period part of the research process. Nested time-series validation can help organise this separation when many choices are compared.

Costs, benchmarks and reporting

Calculate turnover from the actual drifted pre-trade weights. Include transaction costs, spreads, borrowing costs and any relevant market impact. Compare against transparent policies such as equal weight or a feasible minimum-variance allocation with the same dates, universe and accounting conventions.

Report realised volatility, mean excess return, drawdowns, turnover, gross exposure and uncertainty rather than a single ratio. Annualised Sharpe scaling by H\sqrt H assumes a suitable serial-dependence structure; autocorrelation and overlapping observations can invalidate that shortcut.

The study by DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal motivates careful comparison with simple diversification in the presence of estimation error. Its empirical results concern tested strategies and datasets, not a theorem that equal weights are always optimal.

Single-period theory and dynamic choice

Repeatedly solving a one-period problem is a myopic policy. It does not automatically solve a dynamic investment problem with changing opportunities, liabilities, trading costs or intertemporal hedging demands. The classical model remains valuable as a clear baseline, provided its scope is not extended by implication.

25 / Interactive study

Interactive efficient-frontier laboratory

Change the three assets' annual expected simple returns, volatilities and pairwise correlations. Choose unrestricted or long-only investment, an exact target return, a same-horizon risk-free return and a risk-aversion coefficient. The laboratory recomputes the opportunity set and the relevant portfolios from those inputs.

Volatilities and means are entered as percentages; correlations are unitless. The covariance matrix is constructed as Σij=σiσjρij\Sigma_{ij}=\sigma_i\sigma_j\rho_{ij}. Invalid or nearly singular correlation matrices are rejected. Unrestricted weights have no gross-exposure cap; long-only weights cannot be negative.

Reading the results

The chart shows the selected feasible minimum-variance boundary, with upper and lower branches labelled separately. GMV, the exact-target portfolio and a conventional positive-Sharpe tangency portfolio are marked when available. The weights table identifies the same portfolios, and target risk shares decompose its forecast variance.

A target below the selected GMV mean is feasible in some cases but dominated. An unavailable long-only target does not erase the rest of the opportunity set; its row is labelled infeasible. For unrestricted investment, conventional positive tangency requires rf<μGMVr_f<\mu_{\mathrm{GMV}}. Long-only tangency is searched on feasible faces and requires positive expected excess return.

Suggested experiments

Begin with the benchmark and reduce correlation AC while preserving matrix admissibility. Observe the changes in GMV volatility and weights. Then raise the target from 10% toward 14% and compare unrestricted with long-only weights. Beyond 14%, the long-only target becomes infeasible, while unrestricted extrapolation requires short positions.

Increase A's expected return by one percentage point without changing covariance, and inspect the tangency weights. Then change only risk aversion: the tangency recipe stays fixed while the indicated cash allocation changes. These experiments isolate inputs; they do not estimate how real market parameters move together.

Set all expected returns equal to inspect the degenerate frontier. Supply individually plausible but mutually incompatible correlations to see why pairwise bounds are insufficient. All calculations run offline. Hover, tap or use the chart's arrow keys to inspect the curves without changing the inputs.

A concentration cap

With each weight bounded above by 60%, the smallest feasible mean is 0.6(0.06)+0.4(0.10)=7.6%0.6(0.06)+0.4(0.10)=7.6\%. The largest is 0.6(0.14)+0.4(0.10)=12.4%0.6(0.14)+0.4(0.10)=12.4\%. A target of 13% is infeasible under those caps even though it is feasible without them.

This calculation checks feasibility independently of the optimiser. It also distinguishes a concentration cap from a short-sale restriction. A solver should identify the reason a target fails, rather than returning a renormalised approximation with a different expected return.
